CausalChain: NAFLD-induced metabolic stress -> Upregulation of FTO demethylase in hepatocytes -> Site-specific removal of m6A marks on mRNAs (and select ncRNAs) encoding lipid metabolism regulators -> Increased stability and translation of these lipid-regulatory transcripts -> Altered lipogenesis and metabolic reprogramming -> Predisposition of hepatocytes to malignant transformation -> Development of HCC
Hypothesis: In NAFLD-driven liver disease, metabolic stress upregulates the m6A demethylase FTO which, via site-specific demethylation of m6A marks on mRNAs encoding key lipid metabolism regulators, enhances transcript stability and promotes their efficient translation. This process reprograms hepatocyte metabolism—by augmenting lipogenesis and altering energy homeostasis—and primes cells for malignant transformation. Moreover, we hypothesize that FTO-mediated epitranscriptomic reprogramming acts in concert with dysregulation of noncoding RNAs, adding an additional layer of regulation during the NAFLD-to-HCC transition. We plan to leverage technologies such as m6A-RIP sequencing to map the precise m6A landscape, CRISPR-based tools for modulating FTO activity, and RNA stability assays to validate target specificity, thereby clarifying the mechanistic interplay between FTO activity and lipid metabolic reprogramming.
Abstract: We hypothesize that in NAFLD-driven liver disease, upregulation of the m6A demethylase FTO leads to a selective, site-specific removal of m6A modifications on key mRNAs encoding lipid metabolism regulators, such as those involved in lipogenesis and energy homeostasis. This demethylation increases the stability and translation of these transcripts, thereby reprogramming hepatocyte metabolism and facilitating the progression from NAFLD to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Importantly, we propose that this mechanism is intertwined with perturbations in noncoding RNA (ncRNA) regulation, suggesting a coordinated epitranscriptomic network driving malignant transformation. We further propose to employ contemporary high-throughput techniques—such as m6A-RIP sequencing, CRISPR-mediated epitranscriptomic editing, and RNA stability assays—to robustly identify candidate transcript targets and mechanistic binding co-factors that dictate FTO’s site-specific activity. This integrated approach will enhance our understanding of how FTO-driven demethylation intricately modulates both mRNAs and select ncRNAs to prime hepatocytes for a shift toward tumorigenic metabolism.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on FTO-mediated removal of m6A marks from mRNAs encoding lipid metabolism regulators leading to transcript stabilization and metabolic reprogramming. The revised hypothesis retains this core concept but integrates several enhancements: (1) It explicitly incorporates the role of altered noncoding RNA (ncRNA) regulation as an added layer that may interact with mRNA demethylation. (2) It emphasizes the need for site-specificity by proposing the identification of candidate transcripts and corresponding binding co-factors. (3) It outlines the practical application of contemporary technologies (e.g., m6A-RIP sequencing, CRISPR-based epitranscriptomic editing, and RNA stability assays) to examine the mechanistic details. (4) The revised causal chain now explicitly reflects the interplay between mRNAs and ncRNAs, thereby addressing broader observations in HCC and providing a more comprehensive, testable framework that is logically coherent and experimentally tractable.
